original_question: Does there exist an extremal positive ddc-closed current T directed by a foliation F for which one can estimate the speed at which the Nevanlinna currents τ_r^a converge to T in Theorem 2.1 when tested against smooth observables θ?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2.2(ii), in the setting of Theorem 2.1.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target. It has the correct existential form ('does there exist'), the correct object (an extremal positive dd^c-closed current T directed by a foliation F), the correct convergence object (the Nevanlinna currents τ_r^a from Theorem 2.1), and the correct quantitative emphasis (estimating the speed of convergence when testing against smooth observables).
missing_details: The ambient setting from the lead-in to Theorem 2.1 is missing: F is a possibly singular foliation by Riemann surfaces on a compact Kähler manifold X equipped with a fixed Kähler form ω.
The paper assumes, for simplicity in Theorem 2.1, that T has full mass on the hyperbolic leaves; this hypothesis is part of the local context for the question.
The convergence theorem whose rate is being quantified is stated under the hypothesis that all singularities of F are linearizable.
The quantifier 'for T-almost every a' is essential in Theorem 2.1 and should be carried into a stand-alone version of the question.
The notation τ_r^a should be unpacked: a lies on a hyperbolic leaf L_a, φ^a: D -> L_a is the universal covering with φ^a(0)=a, and τ_r^a is the associated Nevanlinna current.
The asymptotic regime should be stated explicitly: τ_r^a converges to T as r -> 1.
The paper’s 'smooth observables' are not arbitrary functions in the statement of Theorem 2.1; they are smooth test forms θ of bi-degree (1,1) on X, paired with currents via <τ_r^a, θ>.
If one wants full self-containment, the operator should be identified as dd^c = (i/π)∂∂̄, as recalled in the introduction.
If one wants full self-containment, 'directed by F' should be glossed as tangent to the foliation in the sense recalled in the introduction.
The paper does not ask for such an estimate for every extremal directed positive dd^c-closed current; it asks only whether there exists one such T.
The nearby context adds that a current of positive entropy is considered a good candidate for T; this is part of the paper-faithful scope around the problem.
refined_question: In the setting of Theorem 2.1, let F be a possibly singular foliation by Riemann surfaces on a compact Kähler manifold X with Kähler form ω, and let T be an extremal positive dd^c-closed current (dd^c = (i/π)∂∂̄) directed by F, assumed for simplicity to have full mass on the hyperbolic leaves. For a point a on a hyperbolic leaf L_a, let φ^a: D -> L_a be the universal covering with φ^a(0)=a, and let τ_r^a be the associated Nevanlinna current. Assuming that all singularities of F are linearizable so that τ_r^a -> T as r -> 1 for T-almost every a, does there exist such an extremal directed positive dd^c-closed current T for which one can quantitatively estimate the speed of convergence of <τ_r^a, θ> to <T, θ> for smooth test forms θ of bi-degree (1,1) on X?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 2 rather than the paper’s Section 1 problems: it closely paraphrases the second part of Problem 2.2, which is posed immediately after Theorem 2.1 and asks whether one can estimate the speed of the convergence from that theorem for smooth observables. The theorem’s surrounding paragraph supplies the hidden assumptions and notation that make the question stand alone: the compact Kähler ambient manifold, the foliation by Riemann surfaces, the extremal directed positive dd^c-closed current T, the assumption that T has full mass on hyperbolic leaves, the universal-cover parametrization of a leaf, and the fact that the convergence holds for T-almost every a under linearizable singularities. The sentence immediately after Problem 2.2 adds that a current of positive entropy is a good candidate for T. I therefore kept the question existential and narrow, and only imported the hypotheses needed to state faithfully what quantitative convergence question the paper actually asks.
